fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because honestly a big fraction of my own work has been about showing that claimed benefits don't hold up. So I'm maybe more paranoid than most people.

The first thing I want to see is a controlled baseline. That sounds obvious, but it's the thing that gets violated most often. When someone introduces a new architecture, they usually introduce it together with a new training recipe. Different optimizer, different augmentation, longer schedule, different regularization. And then the comparison is against a baseline number pulled from a paper that was written five years ago with the old recipe. So you have two things changing at once, and the paper attributes everything to the architecture. When we did ConvNeXt, the whole starting point was: take a plain ResNet-50, give it the same training recipe that Swin Transformer or DeiT uses, and see what happens. And just doing that moved the ResNet by several points before we touched the architecture at all. So a large part of what people thought was "transformers beat convnets" was actually "the 2021 recipe beats the 2015 recipe." I'd want the baseline retrained under the exact same conditions. If the authors didn't do that, I don't really know what I'm looking at.

Second, I want the comparison to be matched on something that matters for the practitioner. Parameters, FLOPs, actual throughput on a GPU, training compute. Ideally more than one of those, because they tell different stories. There are many architectures that look great on FLOPs and are terrible on wall-clock, because the operations are memory-bound or don't parallelize well. If the gain is only visible on one axis and disappears on the others, that's a sign it's more of an accounting trick than a real benefit.

Third, and this is the one I care about most, I want to see how it behaves across scale. A lot of architectural tricks help a lot at small scale and then wash out. Inductive biases are the classic example: they help when data is limited and the gap closes or reverses when you have more data and more compute. So I'd like to see the curve, not a single point. If I only get a single point, I'd at least want to see it at a scale that's representative of how people would actually use the thing.

Then there's the question of variance. On ImageNet, the run-to-run noise for a ResNet-50 is something like a tenth or two tenths of a percent, so if your improvement is 0.3 and you reported one seed, I'm not convinced. For smaller datasets the noise is much bigger. I'd rather see multiple seeds and an honest error bar, and if the improvement is inside the noise, just say so.

And finally, does it transfer? Does the thing that helps on ImageNet classification also help on detection, segmentation, or whatever downstream task the model is supposed to be a backbone for? Does it survive being fine-tuned? One of the lessons from the pruning work we did was that a lot of results that look very solid in one setting completely evaporate when you change the evaluation protocol slightly. So if an architecture change only helps in exactly the setting it was tuned on, I'd treat it as a result about that setting, not about the architecture.

I should say, this is a high bar, and I don't think everyone needs to clear every item in every paper. But if I'm deciding whether to actually adopt something in my own work, that's roughly the checklist. Same recipe, matched cost, more than one scale, more than one seed, more than one task. If it survives all of that, I believe it. If it only survives one of them, I'll still read the paper, but I'm probably not changing what I use.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is a really controlled comparison. A lot of the time when a new architecture comes out, it's compared against a baseline that was trained years earlier with a much weaker recipe: fewer epochs, older augmentation, a different optimizer, less regularization. Then it's very hard to tell whether the gain comes from the architecture or from everything else that changed.

That was a big motivation behind our ConvNeXt work. When vision transformers started beating ResNets, a natural question was how much of that was really the attention mechanism, and how much was the training recipe and design choices that came along with transformers. When we just took a standard ResNet and trained it with a modern recipe, it already improved by a couple of points, before touching the architecture at all. Then we modernized it step by step and ended up competitive with Swin transformers while staying a pure ConvNet. So a lot of what people attributed to "transformers vs. ConvNets" was actually confounded.

So the first thing I'd want is that both the baseline and the new model get the same training budget, the same data, the same recipe, and a comparable amount of tuning effort. If you swept learning rates for your method, you should sweep them for the baseline too. I'd also want the comparison to be roughly matched in compute or parameters, because almost anything gets better if it's bigger.

Second, I'd want to see that the gain holds up across scales. Some changes help a small model and disappear at larger scale, or the reverse. If the improvement is consistent across, say, three or four model sizes, that's much more convincing than one data point. And ideally across more than one task or dataset. If something only helps ImageNet classification but not detection, segmentation, or transfer, I'd be a bit suspicious that it's overfitting to that benchmark.

Third, just basic statistics. Run multiple seeds and report the variance. In a lot of settings the seed-to-seed noise is a few tenths of a percent, and many papers claim improvements that are about that size. If the gain is smaller than the noise, it's not really a result.

And finally, I like to see ablations that tell you *why* it works. If you add three components and get a gain, which one is actually responsible? Sometimes it turns out to be something mundane, like an extra normalization layer or a different initialization, rather than the main idea of the paper. We saw something like this with network pruning too: people believed the pruned weights inherited from the large model were important, but when you train the pruned architecture from scratch with a proper schedule, you often get the same or better accuracy. The real value was in the architecture, not the weights.

So my bar is basically: fair baseline, same recipe, multiple scales, multiple tasks, multiple seeds, and ablations that isolate the cause. If a change survives all of that, I'd believe it's real. Honestly, very few changes do, and I think that says something about how robust the basic designs we already have are.

fable-5.text:
That's a question I care a lot about, because I think our field has historically been pretty sloppy here. So let me give you a few things I'd want to see.

The first and most important one is that the comparison has to be controlled, and in particular the baseline has to be given the same love as the new architecture. What happens very often is that someone proposes a new architecture, they tune it carefully — the learning rate, the augmentation, the training length, all the modern tricks — and then they compare against a baseline number copied from a paper that's three or five years old, trained with a much weaker recipe. Actually, part of the motivation for our ConvNeXt work was exactly this: when we took a standard ResNet and just trained it with a modern recipe, the accuracy jumped by several points without changing the architecture at all. So a lot of what gets attributed to architecture is really attributable to training. Before I believe an architecture claim, I want to see the old and new architectures trained under the same recipe, with comparable tuning effort on both sides.

Second, the comparison should be matched on resources. Same parameter count, or same FLOPs, or same actual throughput on hardware — ideally you report all of them, because they can tell different stories. If your new block is better but also twice as expensive, you haven't shown an architectural benefit, you've shown that more compute helps, which we already knew.

Third, I want to see the benefit hold up across more than one setting. One dataset, one model size, one task — that's an anecdote. If the improvement appears at small scale but shrinks or disappears as you scale up, or it works on ImageNet classification but not when you transfer to detection or segmentation, then it's probably not a fundamental improvement. The architecture changes that have really mattered — residual connections, normalization, attention — they're remarkably robust. They help almost everywhere, at almost every scale. That robustness is, to me, the signature of a real architectural advance.

And then there are a couple of softer criteria. Multiple random seeds, because a half-percent gap on one run is often just noise. And some sensitivity analysis: if the new architecture only wins inside a narrow band of hyperparameters, that fragility itself is a cost, even if the peak number is better.

Honestly, if you apply this bar strictly, the number of architecture changes in the last decade that clear it is smaller than our paper count would suggest. And I don't say that cynically — I say it because it means the baselines are stronger than we think, and the real differentiators are often training, data, and scale. That should shape where we spend our research effort.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, my bar is high, and it's mostly about the baseline rather than the new thing. The first question I ask is: did the old architecture get the same training recipe, the same number of epochs, the same augmentation and regularization, the same hyperparameter search budget? A huge fraction of claimed architectural gains in our field have turned out to be recipe gains in disguise. When we did ConvNeXt, the starting point was exactly that observation — a lot of what people were attributing to attention was really attributable to AdamW, longer schedules, heavy augmentation, LayerScale, and so on. Once you give a plain ConvNet the same treatment, the gap mostly closes. So if someone shows me a two-tenths-of-a-point improvement over a baseline they copied from a 2019 paper, I've learned basically nothing.

Second, I want the comparison matched on compute — parameters and FLOPs, but really wall-clock throughput, because FLOPs can lie badly depending on how memory-bound your operator is. A modification that adds thirty percent latency and buys you half a point isn't an architectural insight, it's a worse point on the same tradeoff curve.

Third, variance. Run multiple seeds. I've seen plenty of "improvements" that sit comfortably inside seed noise on ImageNet, and people just don't report the error bars.

And then the thing I care most about: does it hold up when you change the setting? Different dataset sizes, different model scales, a downstream transfer task. Many tricks help a small model on a small dataset because they're implicitly regularizers, and they vanish — or reverse — when you scale up data or parameters. If the benefit survives all of that, and ideally someone outside the original lab reproduces it, then I'll believe the architecture is actually doing something.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I'd want a few things, and the first is a fair comparison. A lot of architecture papers compare a new design trained with a modern recipe against a baseline trained with an old one. That was part of the motivation for ConvNeXt. When we took a ResNet and gave it the training recipe used for vision transformers, which means longer training, stronger augmentation, AdamW, and so on, it gained a large amount of accuracy before we had changed the architecture at all. So the baseline has to get the same recipe, the same data, and the same compute budget, and ideally its own hyperparameter tuning. Otherwise you can't tell whether the gain comes from the architecture or from everything around it.

Second, I'd want to see that it holds across scales. Many ideas help at small scale and then wash out, or even hurt, once you go bigger. So I'd want several model sizes and more than one point on the compute axis, ideally with the gap staying the same or widening as you scale. A single number at one size isn't very convincing.

Third, seeds and variance. Many reported improvements are within the noise of different random seeds, and people often don't report that. If the gain is 0.2% and the seed-to-seed variation is 0.3%, I don't think we've learned anything.

Fourth, I'd look for breadth. Does it help on other tasks, other modalities, other datasets, or only on the one it was designed around? And I'd care about real cost, not just FLOPs or parameter counts. Throughput on actual hardware and memory use matter, because a change can look efficient on paper and be slower in practice.

Finally, I'd ask whether the change is simple and whether an ablation shows what actually matters. If the architecture has ten new components, I want to know which ones are doing the work. Often the answer is one or two, and the rest is decoration. Simpler ideas that survive all of these checks are the ones I trust, and they tend to be the ones that last. They're also the ones that get adopted by other people.

haiku-5.5.text:
I'd want multiple random seeds first. Run both the baseline and the new architecture several times and look at the spread. On many standard benchmarks, seed-to-seed variance is about the size of the gains people report, so a single run tells you very little.

Second, the baseline has to get the same tuning effort as the new model. It's common to see a proposed architecture with a careful learning-rate sweep, schedule, and weight decay, while the baseline runs on defaults from an older paper. Give both sides the same tuning budget and a lot of the gain often shrinks or disappears.

Third, the comparison should be compute-matched. If the new model uses more FLOPs, parameters, or training data, that needs to be stated and ideally controlled. Otherwise you're mostly measuring that you spent more compute.

Fourth, I want to see whether the effect holds as you scale. A change that helps a small model on a small dataset can vanish or flip at larger scale. A trend across a few model sizes is much more convincing than one good number at one size. And I'd want results on more than the benchmark the design was developed against, since that's where overfitting creeps in without anyone intending it.

Finally, an ablation that isolates the component you credit, along with some explanation of why it helps. If you can't say why a change works, it's hard to believe it will transfer to the next setting.

So the short version is: multiple seeds, equally tuned baselines, matched compute, scaling trends across more than one benchmark, and a clean ablation. If a change clears all of that, I'll take it seriously.

astra-6.text:
I would first want to know whether the improvement actually comes from the architecture. If you change the architecture and also change the training recipe, the data, or the amount of compute, it’s very hard to tell what caused the gain.

So I’d want a strong baseline, with a comparable amount of effort spent tuning it. Then I’d want controlled experiments that isolate the proposed change. That doesn’t necessarily mean using exactly the same hyperparameters for both architectures, because that could favor one of them. But the comparison should give both a fair chance.

I’d also look at whether the benefit holds across runs and across different model sizes or tasks. A small improvement in one setting is useful evidence, but it wouldn’t convince me that the change is broadly better.

And finally, what does the improvement cost? If it adds substantial latency, memory use, or implementation complexity, then I’d need to see a benefit that justifies that tradeoff.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the first question is whether the baseline is strong enough. If you compare a new architecture with an older model using an older training recipe, you don’t really know where the improvement comes from. I would want to put both models under a comparable training setup and give both a reasonable amount of tuning.

Then I’d want to understand the budget. Are we comparing at the same number of parameters, the same training compute, or the same inference latency? Those can give you different answers. A model that gets slightly better accuracy but takes twice as long might still be useful, but you have to make that tradeoff explicit.

And I’d look for consistency: does the gain survive different runs, different model sizes, and perhaps different tasks? Ablations should help isolate which change actually matters. I don’t think an architecture needs to win everywhere, but the evidence should make clear where it helps and whether that improvement is worth the added complexity.
